A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same online linear programming framework. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation results measuring regret and computation time across input distributions, horizons, frequencies, and algorithms in Section 4.

after.justification: V3 retains original simulation results in Section 4 and adds distribution and baseline comparisons in Appendix E.

M1.justification: The hybrid framework and multi-restart extension remain. V3 changes the final-batch learning rate to f^(-2/3), versus f^(-1/2) in v1 Appendix C.3, and describes optional warm-start or LP initialization. Its revised Algorithm 1 also introduces a control-flow inconsistency: the separate LP if/else can overwrite a preceding subgradient update.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds clipped Student's-t resource requests with uniform rewards and a finite-support setting with 50 customer types. These substantially broaden the synthetic input regimes beyond v1's uniform and normal experiments, including evaluation outside the continuous-support setting of the main theory.

E2.justification: Appendix E.2 adds an evaluated infrequent-resolving comparator from Li, Wang, and Zhang (2024). In the retained main comparison, identical score rows formerly labeled 'Offline' and 'First-Order' are identified as classical and restarted first-order methods; these relabelings do not establish two new evaluations.

E3.justification: V3 reports phase-dependent experimental learning rates, replacing the 1/(t+1) prescription in v1's main algorithm listings, although v1's proofs already used different rates. The new finite-support comparison specifies n=50 and comparator parameters alpha=beta=0.95. Original horizon ranges, resource dimensions, capacity sampling, and frequency choices remain; rerunning retained experiments is not established.

E4.justification: The original frequency-sensitivity analyses remain. Appendix E.1 extends the same sweep to clipped Student's-t inputs, adding evidence that the relationship between resolving frequency and regret persists under this additional distribution.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over 100 trials. V3 applies the same practice to its added experiments; neither version reports empirical confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or seed specifications.

E6.justification: Shared main-table values remain unchanged apart from equivalent rounding, while Appendix E adds two substantial result sets. For example, Table 5 reports Algorithm 2 regret 14.30 and runtime 1305.4 seconds at T=10^6, versus 28.80 and 4.929 seconds for infrequent resolving. These are new finite-support results, not a same-setting improvement over v1.

T1.justification: V3 substantially revises Appendix B.3, replacing the reject-all, zero-violation argument with an analysis-only accept-all construction and explicit violation bounds. Theorem B.9 adds a case-based final-batch bound using f^(-2/3), and Lemma B.10 supplies a new warm-start result and proof. These extend the theory beyond relocating existing lemmas.

C1.justification: The central claims remain hybrid LP/first-order decision-making, wait-less operation, and the O(log(T/f)+sqrt(f)) guarantee. The 10-fold regret and 100-fold runtime statements promoted into v3's abstract and contributions already appeared in v1 Section 4.2.

C2.justification: V3 adds a substantive unknown-horizon discussion explaining the fixed-horizon requirement and possible failure of sublinear regret without it. Appendix E.2 also explicitly acknowledges that the proposed methods' lower regret comes with higher computation time than infrequent resolving.

D1.justification: V3 adds an implementation repository link, restarted-baseline pseudocode, and generation and parameter details for the new experiments. Conversely, it omits v1's explicit normal-input relationship r_t=sum_i a_it, leaving that joint distribution less specified; this omission does not establish changed data generation.

R1.justification: V3 adds Balseiro, Kroer, and Kumar (2023) to support the horizon-uncertainty discussion and expands comparison with the already-cited infrequent-resolving work. The broader literature positioning remains similar; publication-year updates and consolidation of duplicate Jiang references do not constitute new research coverage.

P1.justification: The main narrative is extensively condensed, rewritten, and reorganized. Baseline algorithms and preliminary convergence results move into the appendices, the proposed algorithms become Algorithms 1 and 2, and new challenge explanations and a conclusion discussion reshape the exposition.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column conference layout, consolidates the frequency tables, rearranges four plot panels into a horizontal row with shared legends, and expands diagram captions. Appendix E adds two tables and two figures. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: Clearer baseline attribution, broader experiments, warm-start analysis, and the horizon limitation improve the paper's usefulness. However, v3 Algorithm 1 replaces v1's conditional chain with a separate if/else that, read literally, overwrites subgradient updates whenever no LP solve occurs. This conflicts with the retained method description and analysis. The PDFs do not resolve this central specification problem, preventing a reliable judgment of the net quality change.
